diagnosis.summary: Attempt 1 timed out (2100s) before ever completing a Galera bootstrap. The executor spent almost all of its budget fighting package installation on a 32-bit (i686) Ubuntu 16.04 image: the generic `mariadb-server` apt install pulled in `mariadb-server-10.0`, which has no WSREP/Galera support compiled in (no `wsrep` variables, no `galera_new_cluster` binary, no wsrep plugin .so), so the separately-installed `galera-3` package (just the wsrep provider library) was useless without a wsrep-patched mysqld. After discovering this, the executor tried to add MariaDB's official apt repo for `mariadb-10.1` restricted to `arch=i386`, which was slow/timed out at the proxy layer, and a subsequent apt-get update hit a dpkg/apt lock held by the still-running prior apt process — self-inflicted contention from re-issuing apt commands without confirming the earlier one had exited. The maintenance-window task (full shutdown, then restart with data intact) was never reached: mysql was stopped cleanly on node2/node3, but node1's `galera_new_cluster` call failed outright because mysqld wasn't even running (left stopped since the original package postinstall) and the command didn't exist in the installed package.

evidence.finding: `mysqld --no-defaults --verbose --help | grep -i wsrep` returns 0 matches and `grep -i -c galera` returns 0 — the installed mysqld binary has no WSREP/Galera support compiled in.
/usr/lib/mysql/plugin/ contains no wsrep or galera provider .so; installed version is mariadb-server-10.0 (10.0.38-MariaDB, Ubuntu 16.04/xenial).

`sudo galera_new_cluster` → "command not found", and mysql -e query fails with "Can't connect to local MySQL server through socket" — mysqld was not running on node1 and the bootstrap helper script does not exist in this install.

Log shows mysqld starting and immediately shutting down twice during package postinstall (21:36), consistent with the debian package's install-time DB initialization/shutdown, with no subsequent successful start recorded.
Both return exit code 3 / 'inactive', i.e. mysql was successfully stopped cleanly on these two nodes (this part of the shutdown worked).

evidence.source: node1, apt-get update command with MariaDB 10.1 i386 repo
evidence.finding: Command failed with AntriebMCPError: proxy read timeout after 120s while running `apt-get update` against a newly-added `archive.mariadb.org/mariadb-10.1` repo pinned to arch=i386.

A subsequent `sudo apt-get update -qq` failed instantly with 'Could not get lock /var/lib/apt/lists/lock' and `ps aux` still showed the prior apt-get process (pid 16556) and its child /usr/lib/apt/methods workers running — the earlier timed-out command was still executing in the background when the next one was issued.
Nodes report `i686` userspace despite the underlying host CPU being a modern Intel i9 — the OS image is 32-bit, which narrows available upstream Galera/MariaDB package options and repos.

evidence.source: node1/node2 initial apt-get install of mariadb-server mariadb-client galera-3 rsync
evidence.finding: Took well over 30 minutes to complete (polled repeatedly from ~21:22 through ~21:51) — the environment’s package installation/download was very slow even before the wsrep problem was discovered.

likely_causes.cause: Wrong package selected for a Galera deployment: `mariadb-server` on Ubuntu 16.04 installs `mariadb-server-10.0`, which is not built with WSREP/Galera support; `galera-3` alone only supplies the wsrep provider library, not a wsrep-capable mysqld.

Remediation (switching to MariaDB's official 10.1 repo scoped to i386) was attempted but network/repo interaction was slow and hit the platform's 120s proxy timeout, consuming a large fraction of the time budget without completing.

Self-inflicted apt/dpkg lock contention: a new apt command was issued while the previous (proxy-timed-out) apt-get update was still running in the background, causing an immediate lock failure and further delay/confusion.

The overall task exceeded the available time budget largely due to slow package installation/download in this environment (30+ minutes for the initial install alone) combined with the wrong-package rediscovery cycle, not due to any flaw in the shutdown/restart procedure itself, which was never reached in a working state.

32-bit (i686) base image may have narrower/older package availability for Galera-enabled MariaDB, which increases the chance the default distro package lacks wsrep support and that alternate repos are slower or less complete for i386.

next_attempt_guidance: Before installing, verify the exact package needed for a wsrep-capable MariaDB on this OS/arch. On Ubuntu 16.04 the default `mariadb-server-10.0` lacks WSREP; you likely need a MariaDB release known to ship wsrep support for this distro (e.g., a 10.1+ series build with `mariadb-server-10.x` compiled --with-wsrep) or a distro/PPA that provides it — confirm via `mysqld --help --verbose | grep -i wsrep` immediately after install, before proceeding, rather than late in the run.

Check architecture early with `uname -m` / `dpkg --print-architecture` and pick a repo/package combination that has confirmed i386 (or whatever arch is present) coverage; if the official MariaDB repo lacks a fast/complete i386 mirror, consider whether the task's base image can/should be 64-bit, or budget significantly more time for i386-specific downloads.

When a command fails or is reported as failed due to a proxy/timeout error (not a shell exit code), assume the underlying process may still be running remotely — check with `ps aux` / poll before issuing another command that touches the same lock (apt/dpkg), to avoid self-inflicted 'Could not get lock' failures.

Once a wsrep-capable mysqld is confirmed on all three nodes, validate the full stop/start cycle on a low-stakes test (e.g., a scratch database + table) before relying on it for the real maintenance window: stop all three mysqld instances, identify the node with the highest `wsrep_last_committed`/`seqno` from `grastate.dat` (or safest via `--wsrep-recover`), bootstrap only that node (`galera_new_cluster` or equivalent), then start the other two so they SST/IST from the bootstrapped node.

Given the slow package install observed (30+ minutes), front-load and parallelize the apt-get install/update step across all three nodes at the very start of the run so package-fetch time doesn't consume the reasoning/verification budget later, and set a hard internal checkpoint (e.g., abandon/re-plan if wsrep support isn't confirmed within the first several minutes) rather than iterating repo fixes for a long time.
